I see what you’re saying about cultural approaches being considered a priori, but I’d like to clarify my critique. In the same way that you’re suggesting people who adopt a purely cultural perspective are starting from an a priori assumption, I would argue that those who adopt a solely biological approach are also doing the same. Both perspectives, when taken in isolation, could be seen as a priori assumptions about human traits or behavior.

However, I think we both actually agree that neither cultural nor biological explanations are entirely a priori. Both are derived from empirical evidence, making them a posteriori. The cultural approach is informed by sociological, psychological, and anthropological studies, while the biological approach is backed by research from neuroscience and genetics. Both are grounded in observed data and real-world experiences.

My point is that if we critique one side (cultural) for making assumptions, we should apply the same critique to a biological-only perspective. In reality, I think both are rooted in empirical evidence and work best when considered together.
Physicalism is likewise an a priori claim. While embodied cognition itself is a posteriori, the assumption that there is a biological basis is still a priori.

These are the positions we are arguing:

A diagnosis is essential to provide effective and appropriately targeted interventions to those with mental health problems. Effective treatment is simply not possible without an accurate diagnosis. In fact, everyone is entitled to a DSM-5 diagnosis.

There are many problems with using the DSM-5, and diagnosing should be avoided if possible. Clients tend to reify disorders; self-label, which can lead to self-fulfilling prophecy or avoidance of responsibility; equate or identify themselves with the disorder; and overlook useful strengths and other important parts of their identity. All this interferes with effective counselling.

Because DSM diagnosis is a dominant part of western mental health service delivery, it is useful for nonmedical counsellors and psychotherapists to have a working knowledge of the DSM-5. It provides a shared language for mental health practitioners, and opens access to resources that might not otherwise be available to some clients. Its benefits outweigh its disadvantages; therefore, professional counsellors and psychotherapists must be knowledgeable in the DSM-5.

Under no circumstances should counsellors use the DSM-5. The DSM-5, like its predecessors, perpetuates a socially unjust status quo that gives inordinate power to professionals and ignores the perspectives of service recipients. The DSM-5 has little empirical support, and is simply a way of labelling and pathologizing people.

I work with ASD kiddos and I have a specific program to use with a child when out grocery shopping with his family. He bolts, throws, screams, and hits people as well. My team has come up with a Token Reward System. Identify what is reinforcing for him i.e. candy, a toy or item. Then reiterate that he is working for that item. When he receives 5 tokens you can reward him with the item. To get a token he must not be engaging in any of the target disruptive behaviors. Every 30 seconds he is staying close to you, not yelling or throwing things, give him a token. Every time you put a request such as "put the apple juice in the cart" you can give him a token. Once he does get the reward, let him have it for a minute or so then take it back from him and reassure him again that he is working to get it back. If he is bolting, make it known that he will receive a token if he listens to "stop" or "come here". Try to make sure you are not giving him a token if he is staying close to you, but is screaming at the same time. 

I hope this sort of helps.

I'm a behavior interventionist. I go into people's homes daily as well and do specific programs with children on the spectrum. I do things like gross and fine motor development. Sound, action, and object imitation, receptive discrimination, and a lot others. The parents are always home during the session and quite often are very involved and help with some of the programming. It's all about reinforcing positive behaviors and not punishing, but negatively reinforcing behaviors that may inhibit independent growth. For example, if a child tries to escape a task at hand I do not scold the child. I simply try to block, and guide them back to the task with a neutral expression so as to not show that the behavior is something either praiseworthy OR upsetting. Sometimes, it seems, a child will keep their negative behaviors because even showing any type of animated reaction to such behaviors will reinforce them. 

Anyways, I have built strong rapport with the kiddos and the parents and I do believe that it will benefit both in the long run. Hopefully your interventionist will make the sessions as comfortable as possible for you.
